General-purpose classification of the top-level asset class a market
series, instrument, or curve belongs to. The taxonomy's codes and their
prose are declared once, in ores.refdata.asset_class_catalogue, which
also declares the oresmd namespace and the mapping between the two; the
seed SQL this table is populated from is generated from it, so this model
carries no copy of the list. Code carries no parallel enumeration, because
the list is runtime-managed and no compiled list can be exhaustive over
FK-validate against this table. Managed by the system tenant, like other

Describes how ORE builds a bond yield: the compounding it is quoted on, the
frequency it pays at, whether the price is clean or dirty, and the tolerances
its solver runs to. Corresponds to the <BondYield> element in ORE conventions.xml.
The id field is the natural key (ORE <Id> element).
One field is required and six are optional. One file carries five elements and
sets all six optional fields. The accuracy and the guess are floats in ORE and
travel through a double column, because the refdata schema has no float type;
a float widens to a double and narrows back with no loss.

To modify, update the template and regenerate.
One row per family a staging message delivers. The payload is that family's
own generated value type, already serialised, so a stage of one family never
builds a message that carries every family.
The identity is the import, the family and the sequence together. A repeated
stage of the same three is refused rather than duplicated, so a retried stage
is safe. Each stage is its own local transaction, and nothing reaches the
live tables until a commit applies the rows.
AUTO-GENERATED FILE - DO NOT EDIT MANUALLY
To modify, update the template and regenerate.
A bundle is applied in one unit_of_work, and the messages that
carry it cannot hold the whole bundle: a message carrying every family is the
aggregate that fails on MSVC. The import is the row the staging messages hang
off instead. It records that a bundle is being staged, who owns it, how many
families were promised, and when an abandoned session stops waiting.
The caller mints id, so a repeated begin with a known id returns the import
that already exists rather than opening a second one. The service stamps
party_id, state and expires_at from the session it runs in.
Nothing in this table is visible to a reader of the live tables
until a commit applies the staged rows.

One row per (calendar_code, date), produced by the calendar
over a rolling date range, never edited by hand. Read by every
consumer that needs "is date D a business day for calendar C" --
the UI (calendar detail screens, the holiday-aware date picker) and
ORE Studio's own tenor/schedule date-math -- so the answer is
consistent and never requires a live rule evaluation.

One row per dated diary entry on a
central-bank meeting, a scheduled data release, or an open-ended
other event. One table for all event kinds -- never a table per
calendar or per type (settled 2026-08-09, story Decision D1; see
diary_entry_type column classifies the entry via the open-ended
other). Holidays themselves keep their existing machinery
holiday type stays in the vocabulary so the whole classification
lives in one place, even though its physical home is elsewhere.
Template/Instance: an event row is an *instance*; its template is the
(calendar, diary_entry_type, name) triple. A worked case: the FOMC's
eight regularly scheduled meetings per year are entered as a short run
of central_bank_meeting instances on the US.FOMC calendar,
transcribed from the Fed's published calendar with
deferred; calendar_rules's grammar can later feed a template link

One row per one-off override for a single
refdata plumbing. Applies uniformly to *any* calendar -- transcribed
or user-authored, based or base-less: a based calendar's full override
story is entirely calendar.base_calendar_code (which base) plus its
own exception rows (what's different), no separate "adjustment"
concept needed. QuantLib's own irregular, year-gated special dates
(the UK's Jubilee bank holidays, the NYSE's special closings) are
transcribed here, not folded into a
rule stays a timeless, indefinitely-repeating pattern and the
genuinely irregular part of a calendar stays flat, no-logic-at-all

To modify, update the template and regenerate.
ORE names a calendar by text, and its schema fixes the names it accepts: 471
of them, such as TARGET, US settlement, weekends only and currency codes
that stand for a currency's calendar. The schema also accepts two open forms
no list can hold -- any four-letter exchange code such as XNYS, and any name
beginning CUSTOM_ -- and joins of several calendars, written as TARGET,UK
A curve keeps the calendar expression its document wrote, so the export writes
it back unchanged. ores_refdata_validate_calendar_fn splits the expression
and checks each calendar in it against this table or against one of the two
open forms, so a calendar ORE would refuse is refused on insert. The refdata
calendar table models calendars the system materialises; this table is the
vocabulary of names an ORE document may write.

One-off irregular dates (jubilees, special closings) are *not*

Validated enumeration of named date collections consumed by ORE and
and other calendar-shaped reference data. Each row is one concrete
rows, not a joined variant field, so the code column always matches
ORE's XML <Calendar> vocabulary verbatim. Classified by
whose calendar it is — supranational calendars (TARGET) use the
ZZ sentinel (ISO 3166-1's own reserved user-assigned code) rather
than a nullable country reference, since no single country owns them.

A cap and floor volatility entry may name a proxy surface instead of its own
quotes, and ORE states it as a ProxyConfig element inside the entry's
That block was seven nullable columns of the entry, meaningful only when the
entry named a proxy. A row of this part holds it, and a row exists only when the
entry names one, so the presence of the part is the flag and no has_proxy_config
The swaption entry's proxy block is a different element: its source and target
carry ShortSwapIndexBase and SwapIndexBase where this one carries an index
and a rate computation period. It is its own part, swaption_proxy_config, for
that reason: the two share a shape, not a type.

A ProxyConfig builds the surface from another one; it is one per entry, so

for a vanilla CDS. Corresponds to the <CDS> element in ORE conventions.xml.

The settings of one CDSVolatility entry of a curveconfig.xml, one row per
curve_definition in the CDSVolatilities section: the expiries the surface

Its Terms are rows of cds_volatility_term, and the surface it is built as,

To modify, update the template and regenerate.
Describes how ORE builds a constant-maturity-swap spread option: where its
forward starts, how long its underlying swap runs, when it fixes, and the
calendar and conventions its schedule rolls on. Corresponds to the
<CmsSpreadOption> element in ORE conventions.xml. The id field is the natural
All eight fields are required and the corpus sets all eight in all twelve
elements, which are otherwise identical: one convention shared by twelve files.
The two period fields and the spot days stay in ORE's spelling, because they
are tenors rather than frequency enumerations; the day count and the roll
convention are normalised to the canonical codes the other tables hold.
AUTO-GENERATED FILE - DO NOT EDIT MANUALLY
To modify, update the template and regenerate.
The commodities a population may draw from. A commodity trade names its
commodity in free text today, and nothing holds the set a tenant may use, so
a generator that needs one has to invent it.
The code is the name the engine resolves, not a display name: ORE's own
index corpus and example trades spell a commodity as an
exchange-prefixed index, such as NYMEX:CL, ICE:B, XLME:AH or
PM:XAUUSD. The catalogue therefore stores that spelling as its key.
The unit and the quotation currency travel with the commodity because they
are facts about how it trades and not about a particular trade: WTI is
quoted in barrels for dollars, gas in MMBtu for dollars, LME aluminium in
tonnes, gold in ounces. A population that quoted gold per barrel would be
worse than one with no commodity at all.
This model holds the vocabulary only. The forward curves a commodity prices
on are market data, and they are not here.
AUTO-GENERATED FILE - DO NOT EDIT MANUALLY

The settings of one CommodityCurve entry of a curveconfig.xml, one row per
curve_definition in the CommodityCurves section. A commodity curve is built
from forward quotes, or from a base curve and a yield curve, or as a basis over
another commodity curve, or from price segments.
The basis form writes a BasisConfiguration element, whose settings are the
basis_ columns and whose BasisQuotes are rows of curve_quote with that
list name. Price segments are rows of commodity_price_segment. The entry's
own quotes are rows of curve_quote on the entry, and its BootstrapConfig a

starts, how its points are scaled, the calendar it advances on, and whether it
is quoted outright or as a spread to spot. Corresponds to the
<CommodityForward> element in ORE conventions.xml. The id field is the natural
One field is required and seven are optional. Two files carry five elements
between them, and every one sets all seven optional fields except the delivery
AUTO-GENERATED FILE - DO NOT EDIT MANUALLY
To modify, update the template and regenerate.
Describes how ORE builds a commodity future: when it expires, which contract
months it lists, how its expiry anchors to a day of the month or a weekday, and
the schedule of the options written on it. Corresponds to the
<CommodityFuture> element in ORE conventions.xml. The id field is the natural
Thirty of the element's thirty-four fields are modelled here, as forty columns,
because the element's nested structs are flattened rather than given tables of
AnchorDay becomes seven columns, OptionNthWeekday two more, and
OffPeakPowerIndexData four. The corpus uses all six of AnchorDay's variants,
so flattening it is what lets a commodity future round trip at all.
Five files carry the element, in eight hundred and eight elements, and two of
them carried nothing else unmodelled when it landed.
Four more fields hold lists, and each is written as a text column rather than
counted: AveragingData becomes eight columns, and ProhibitedExpiries,
FutureContinuationMappings and OptionContinuationMappings become one text
column each, holding comma-separated dates and from:to pairs. A column is a
weaker home than a table, and it is what keeps the field in the element's
round trip rather than excluding the file from it.

prices come from, its priority, its convention, and its quotes. An off peak

One term of one convention kind, as a screen draws it: the entity and the column
its value travels under, and the leaf of ORE's conventions document that holds it,
named by its schema and its XPath. The XPath is the key of the term's entry in the
ORE parameter contract, which gives the term its label, help, description, default,
format and value set, so none of them is restated here or in a screen.
A kind's terms are what a convention screen shows, in the order the position
states. The first rows come from the mapper that reads and writes the conventions
document, so the column a value is stored in and the element ORE reads it from are
the ones the import and the export already use.

The coded catalogue of convention kinds, one row per convention an ORE
conventions document can carry. A central convention row names its kind with
this code, and the kind selects the family whose parts the row carries.
The rows are ORE's own convention category names, upper-cased: the kind of
tenor_basis_swap_convention is TENOR_BASIS_SWAP. A kind that is modelled
beside this table in ores.refdata owns a family of parts; this table is the
closed set that says which kinds the central row may be.
Batch-loaded reference data, refreshed from ORE's ore_types.xsd alongside the
AUTO-GENERATED FILE - DO NOT EDIT MANUALLY
To modify, update the template and regenerate.
The central row of the atomised convention. Every convention kind -- a swap, a
deposit, a tenor basis swap -- is one row here plus the parts its family names.
The row carries the key, the party that owns the row, the kind the row is, and
the name it carries in the source document.
The name is the identifier the source document gives the convention, the <Id>
element of that document. It is kept so a round trip through the ORE XML is
lossless, and it is part of the convention's identity: the party, the kind and
the name together are what make a convention the one a caller means. Two kinds
may hold the same name, because the kind is part of that identity.
A convention's kind-specific fields live in that kind's parts, reached from
this row by its key. The central row carries no kind-specific column.

A credit limit is the amount of credit the firm allows one counterparty,
set by one legal entity of the firm. It is the dimension that splits a
: where one agreement covers trades under several limits,
netting is restricted to the trades within one limit (see
The limit is a credit fact, not a legal one, so it stands apart from the
agreement: one agreement may cover several limits, and one limit may
cover trades under several agreements. A netting set names both, and a
pinned key holds the set's counterparty and party to the limit's, as it

Cross Currency Basis Flat Leg Table
The leg of a cross-currency basis swap that pays its index flat, as ORE's
FlatIndex with the Flat* fixing rules: whether the index is resettable,
the tenor, the payment lag, whether the spread is included in the coupon, the
lookback, the fixing days, the rate cutoff, whether coupons are averaged, and
whether the observation is shifted. They are a part because each states how
this one leg builds its coupon; the spread leg beside it states its own. Each
column keeps the flat_ prefix of ORE's element, because the screen shows
both legs of one convention on one row, and the two legs' columns would
AUTO-GENERATED FILE - DO NOT EDIT MANUALLY
To modify, update the template and regenerate.
Cross Currency Basis Spread Leg Table
The leg of a cross-currency basis swap that pays its index plus the basis
spread, as ORE's SpreadIndex with the Spread* fixing rules: the tenor, the
payment lag, whether the spread is included in the coupon, the lookback, the
fixing days, the rate cutoff, whether coupons are averaged, and whether the
observation is shifted. They are a part because each states how this one leg
builds its coupon; the flat leg beside it states its own. Each column keeps the
spread_ prefix of ORE's element, for the reason the flat leg's columns do.
AUTO-GENERATED FILE - DO NOT EDIT MANUALLY
To modify, update the template and regenerate.
Cross Currency Basis Swap Terms Table
The terms a cross-currency basis swap states once for both legs, as ORE's
IsResettable. It is a part because its fields hold one invariant: each
applies to the whole swap at once, so neither leg can hold it alone. The
settlement fields fix the settlement date, the roll convention and the end of
month rule roll the schedules of both legs, and the resettable flag resets the
notional of the swap. The flat and spread legs beside it hold none of them.
AUTO-GENERATED FILE - DO NOT EDIT MANUALLY
To modify, update the template and regenerate.
Cross Currency Fix Float Fixed Leg Table
The leg a cross-currency fix-float swap pays in the currency it fixes, as
FixedDayCounter. It is a part because its four fields hold one invariant: the
terms the fixed leg is built from, and a convention either states them or does
not. The floating leg beside it holds none of them.
AUTO-GENERATED FILE - DO NOT EDIT MANUALLY
To modify, update the template and regenerate.
Cross Currency Fix Float Float Leg Table
The leg a cross-currency fix-float swap pays off an index, as ORE's Index
with its fixing rules: whether the index is resettable, whether the spread is
included in the coupon, the lookback, the fixing days, the rate cutoff, whether
coupons are averaged, and whether the observation is shifted. They are a part
because a convention that states the floating leg states that block or none of
it; the fixed leg beside it holds none of them.
AUTO-GENERATED FILE - DO NOT EDIT MANUALLY
To modify, update the template and regenerate.
Cross Currency Fix Float Swap Terms Table
The terms a cross-currency fix-float swap states once for both legs, as ORE's
IsResettable. It is a part because its fields hold one invariant: each
applies to the whole swap at once, so neither leg can hold it alone. The
settlement fields fix the settlement date, the end of month rule rolls the
